newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan paves way for breakup of NTT.
newsitem.headline: Japan paves way for breakup of NTT.

text.p: The biggest legal and tax hurdles to the breakup of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp. were cleared this week, paving the way for the world's largest telephone company to start splitting itself into pieces.
The ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) Wednesday formally endorsed a plan to give NTT tax breaks after its planned breakup in 1999.

This followed an announcement by the government on Tuesday that it would lift a 50-year ban on holding companies as early as next January, allowing NTT to be broken up into one international and long-distance carrier and two regional firms, under a holding company structure.
A holding company has control of one or more other companies, usually through stock ownership, but does not itself engage in a specific business.
The ban on such firms was introduced by U.S. forces after World War II as they believed that big conglomerates known as "zaibatsu" contributed to Japan's war effort.
For NTT, resolving the tax and holding company issue was vital to its breakup, which was decided on in December after lengthy negotiations with the Posts and Telecommunications Ministry.
"To be honest, we had expected it to take much more time to resolve such big problems," NTT President Junchiro Miyazu told a news conference.
Miyazu added, however, that the formal breakup of the company would not come before it was approved at a shareholders' meeting although NTT hoped to complete most of its restructuring before then.
"Our intention is to move as quickly as possible, but it looks as though it will be difficult to complete the restructuring business by next year's shareholders' meeting," Miyazu said.
Under Japanese law, the reorganized firms companies would have had to face heavy taxes on land transfers.
But an LDP commission decided to exempt NTT from the asset-transfer tax on the grounds that its breakup is in line with government policy.
The LDP has also decided to allow NTT's planned regional carrier that will cover east Japan, including Tokyo, to use its profits to offset possible losses of its other carrier covering western Japan.
That measure, which would reduce the tax burden on NTT, will take effect for the three years following the restructuring.
Bills to remove the holding company ban and to split NTT will be submitted to parliament on March 11.
